1 — What we count

  • Audited node count: the number of nodes that revealed (submitted a storage proof) in at least one audit round with an agreed result in the 30 days to the date. A node is a staking account; moving to a new address does not change it.
  • N-day BOTD (benefit of the doubt) count: the audited count plus the nodes that registered or moved to a new address in the N days to the date and have not revealed there yet. Of the 940 new or moved addresses since September 2025 that revealed within 90 days, 99.6% did so within 30 days and 93.3% within 14.

Past behaviour

The first chart shows how long nodes that registered or moved to a new address since September 2025 took to pass their first audit: the cumulative share that had passed by each day, among those that passed within 90 days. Within 90 days, 343 of 540 new nodes and 597 of 647 moved addresses passed an audit at all. Height-1 nodes are audited twice as often as height-0 nodes and so tend to pass sooner. The dotted line is the model of time to first passed audit used in the Component model forecast (§4.2): no audit is passed for a sync time of s days after registering, followed by the wait for an audit at height 0. The forecast uses s = 1 day; the slider changes s in this chart only.

s = 0 days. Mean distance of the model curve from the data, days 0–7: 9 percentage points (new nodes), 4 (moved addresses); days 0–30: 4 and 2.

s = 0.5 days. Mean distance of the model curve from the data, days 0–7: 10 percentage points (new nodes), 3 (moved addresses); days 0–30: 5 and 2.

s = 1 day. Mean distance of the model curve from the data, days 0–7: 12 percentage points (new nodes), 8 (moved addresses); days 0–30: 6 and 3.

s = 1.5 days. Mean distance of the model curve from the data, days 0–7: 17 percentage points (new nodes), 12 (moved addresses); days 0–30: 7 and 5.

s = 2 days. Mean distance of the model curve from the data, days 0–7: 21 percentage points (new nodes), 17 (moved addresses); days 0–30: 9 and 6.

The second chart shows the distribution of lengths of runs of consecutive missed audits by nodes that had previously passed an audit, for runs starting since 10 December 2025. Length is measured in audits (left) and in days between the passes either side of the run (right). The last bar includes 492 runs still open on 28 October. Another 571 runs still open with fewer than 12 misses are not shown.

3 — Notable events, October 2026

  • 9 Oct: Last reveal by any of the 512 addresses registered on 11 September; none has revealed since.
  • 11 Oct: 20 new nodes at height 2, 40 BZZ each; 20 have revealed.
  • 14–15 Oct: 2,048 new nodes at height 0, 10 BZZ each; 1,527 have revealed. These nodes were deployed by the Swarm Foundation to stabilise the network and the storage price ahead of the anticipated storage depth increase from 9 to 10.
  • 16 Oct: Storage depth rose from 9 to 10 (1,024 neighbourhoods). A height-0 node is now audited about 3 times in 30 days instead of 6.
  • 16–18 Oct: 241 existing nodes moved to new addresses, 235 of them silent for more than 30 days before; 200 have revealed since.
  • 19 Oct: 38 new nodes at height 1, 20–90 BZZ; 31 have revealed.

4 — Forecast models

We consider two forecast models: the Direct fit (§4.1) and the Component model (§4.2).

How the models are assessed

Each model is refitted at every weekly origin back to March 2026, using only data up to that origin, and its forecasts are compared with the counts later observed. The diagnostics tables report the following for each forecast horizon. The 34-day horizon is that of the 30 November forecast.
  • In 80% range: the share of observed counts that fell inside the forecast's 80% range. It should be near 80%.
  • MAE (mean absolute error): the mean absolute difference, in nodes, between the median forecast and the observed count.
  • Naive forecast: a forecast that the count does not change from its value at the origin.
  • Naive MAE: the MAE of the naive forecast. A model whose MAE is above the naive MAE does worse than assuming no change.

4.1 — Direct fit

How it works

  • RPN (revenue per node) is the USD value of the BZZ paid to nodes in the 7 days to a date, per audited node per day. It was USD 0.031 on 27 October.
  • We fit a linear model of the daily change in the node count \(X_t\) (audited, or N-day BOTD) on log RPN by least squares, on every day from 10 December 2025 (the first full window after the November 2025 depth change) to 27 October 2026:
\[X_t - X_{t-1} = \alpha + \beta \log \mathrm{RPN}_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t.\]
  • For forecasting, RPN is held at its 27 October value and each day ahead adds the fitted drift plus a residual resampled from the fitted residuals.
  • Resampling the residuals means that occasional events, such as unusually large batches of node registrations, are forecast to recur at roughly their past rate, except for the part explained by RPN.

β has the expected sign: higher RPN is associated with more node entries. The estimate is very noisy, however: its standard error is about as large as β or larger."Days with a residual above 50 in size" counts the days on which the count moved by more than 50 nodes beyond what the model predicts, typically large batch registrations. Resampling the residuals replays jumps of this size in the forecast at the same frequency.

Limitations

  • RPN shows no clear effect. Fitted from 1 October 2025, across the November 2025 depth change, β turns negative.
  • RPN is held constant over the forecast, which is unrealistic. This could easily be improved by holding total revenue constant and recomputing RPN from the simulated node count, or by adjusting total revenue by the storage price.
  • Days are drawn independently, so a batch that comes online over several days recurs only by chance, and busy spells do not cluster.
  • The model sees only the history of the count, not which nodes make it up. It cannot anticipate that the BOTD credit for October registrations that have not passed an audit expires at the end of the grace period, or that the audited count will fall from mid-November, when its 30-day window covers only audits after the depth change and nodes are audited half as often.
  • The median forecast was worse than the naive forecast at every horizon in the backtest.

4.2 — Component model

How it works

The Component model simulates, node by node, which nodes pass an audit in the window counted on each day. Probability to pass an audit is based on the length of the current run of missed audits, with probabilities taken from the sampling distribution. New registrations are simulated by resampling, given one day of downtime, and then treated the same as a healthy node. The pass rates out of sample: fitted on audits to 29 July, against the rates seen after.
misses in a row (height 0)012345
fitted to 29 Jul0.930.830.690.260.030.01
seen after (audits)0.91 (18,491)0.74 (1,467)0.50 (301)0.19 (104)0.19 (57)0.14 (29)
With around 30 forecasts per horizon, which overlap in time, a coverage of 74% against a nominal 80% is within sampling error. Coverage of the BOTD counts falls further below 80% at longer horizons and longer grace periods, because a BOTD count credits a batch registration in full on the day it registers, so a batch the simulation did not draw falls far outside the range.

Limitations

  • Given its height and run of missed audits, whether a node passes its next audit is independent of every other node. The model may therefore fail to capture operators taking whole fleets of nodes up or down at once.
  • Every simulated new node has the same 64% chance of ever coming online, pooled over all past registrations. A whole batch failing to come online, like the 512 nodes registered on 11 September, is not simulated.
  • A node with 12 or more consecutive missed audits has no chance of passing, so the model never forecasts a long-dormant node returning.
  • Batch arrivals do not depend on RPN; that has not been tested.
  • The pass rates were estimated mostly from audits at storage depth 9. Since the depth increase, nodes are audited half as often, and the pass rates per audit may no longer hold.
